summary.text: Niobe queen of Thebes, daughter of Tantalus and wife of Amphion, boasted that her seven sons and seven daughters surpassed the children of Leto — and Apollo and Artemis answered with arrows until every child was dead, Amphion fell on his sword, and grief turned Niobe herself to weeping stone on Sipylus.

chapters.title: The boast
chapters.text: The Theban women were wreathed with laurel for Latona when Manto daughter of Tiresias cried that the goddess commanded worship — but Niobe, rich in husband, lineage, and kingdom, refused. She had known Arachne's fate in Maeonia and learned nothing: she counted her children — seven sons and seven daughters in Ovid, though Homer remembers six of each and Apollodorus catalogues rival totals from Hesiod and Herodorus — and mocked Latona for bearing only two.

chapters.title: The arrows
chapters.text: Leto appealed to her twins; Phoebus and Phoebe descended on Thebes in cloud. On the plain Niobe's sons rode their horses — Ismenus, Sipylus, Phaedimus, Tantalus, and the rest — and Apollo's shafts struck them one by one. At the palace Artemis slew the daughters as they mourned; Niobe spread her arms over the youngest and cried, leave me one! — but the last child died in that embrace.

chapters.title: The weeping stone
chapters.text: Childless beside the corpses of sons, daughters, and husband, Niobe grew chill as marble; her tears still flowed while a whirlwind bore her to her native mountain on Sipylus, where she stands as stone that drips forever. Ovid leaves her utterly bereft; Apollodorus and Hyginus preserve survivors — a son Amphion or Amyclas, a daughter Chloris or Meliboea — so the house of Tantalus is not always extinguished.
